More confrontational: Irans new hardline security leadership
Iraq struggles to disarm militias amid US-Iran tug-of-war
item.description:
Esmail Qaani has a habit of not announcing his visits to Baghdad. He simply appears, meets whoever needs meeting, and leaves before most Iraqis know he was there.

His trip on August 10 was no different. The commander of Iran’s Quds Force, the branch of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responsible for backing armed allies abroad, met with Iraqi militia commanders and officials from the Coordination Framework, the alliance of Iran-aligned Shia parties that dominate Iraq’s parliament and effectively chose the current prime minister.

Qaani reportedly pressed the militants to keep their weapons rather than hand them to the government. The Iraqi government, laboring under intense American pressure, has set a September 30 deadline for all militias operating outside state authority to disarm. On that same day, U.S. forces are scheduled to withdraw from their last bases in Iraq

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who has publicly aligned more closely with the U.S. than Iran, did not receive Qaani. According to one source close to the premier who spoke to MBN, al-Zaidi “wants a political relationship, not a military one.”

Two days after Qaani arrived, another story broke about Washington. Asharq al-Awsat reported that al-Zaidi’s cabinet, sworn in three months ago, still had nine ministries unfilled, including defense and interior. The reason? Tom Barrack, America’s ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Iraq and Syria, has been vetoing candidates for the posts, according to the report.

Barrack’s redlines are not limited to groups that command fighters directly. They reportedly extend to the political coalition of Nouri al-Maliki, the former prime minister whose bloc fields no militia of its own but has long governed in a coalition with the factions Washington wants disarmed. Notably, President Donald Trump had warned in January that the “United States will no longer help Iraq” if al-Maliki was reinstalled, blaming him for “total chaos” — a reference to the political purges and sectarian policies of the Maliki era that helped ISIS seize a third of the country in 2014.

Barrack’s veto, then, is reinforcing a line Trump already drew publicly, sending the message that proximity to the militias also disqualifies candidates.

While Washington and Tehran engage in a tug of war over Iraq’s weapons, al-Zaidi has asked parliament’s defence and security committee to draft legislation that would formally place all weapons under exclusive government control. Failure to disarm by the September 30 deadline could be met with terrorism charges.

The bill would remove a legal grey zone that has let the Popular Mobilization Forces, an umbrella of mostly Shia militias that Iraq formally absorbed into its security apparatus in 2016, operate for decades as simultaneously part of the state, but answerable to no one in it. Whether the bill can pass a parliament stocked with the very factions it targets is another matter entirely.

All of this is unfolding amid the ongoing war between the U.S. and Iran. On February 28, Israel and the U.S. struck Iran, opening a war whose aftershocks continue to reverberate. Iran’s supreme leader was killed in the opening strikes; his body was carried through the Iraqi holy cities of Najaf and Karbala last month in processions that drew crowds shouting “Death to America” and “Death to Israel,” a stark reminder of how thoroughly Iraq remains bound to Iran, even as its new premier tries to distance his country from the Islamic Republic.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which Iraq once shipped the vast majority of its oil, remains largely closed. Oil revenue (accounting for roughly 90% of the state budget) has collapsed by roughly two-thirds since the war began, and Baghdad has struggled to pay public-sector salaries.

To keep crude moving, Iraq has reportedly been selling oil at a steep discount (as much as $30 a barrel below benchmark) to Abu Dhabi’s state oil firm, ADNOC, which ferries the crude out of the strait by going “dark” — turning off transponders to evade detection by Iran’s navy.

It was against that backdrop of economic and geopolitical tension that al-Zaidi flew on July 14 to Washington, where he secured a warm Oval Office reception. Trump called him “young and handsome” and touted their “tremendous chemistry.” Al-Zaidi also secured a raft of energy deals and pledged that all weapons would come under state control, an unrealistic claim that was nevertheless music to Trump’s ears.

So far, progress on this front has been halting.Two factions, Asaib Ahl al-Haq and Kataib Imam Ali, announced they would sever ties to the Popular Mobilization Forces and place their weapons under state authority. However, Mohammed A. Salih, writing for The New Region, notes that Iraqi media reporting has found the handover ceremonies involved mostly scrap weapons, and that no independent mechanism exists to verify that heavier weapons — drones, missiles and the like — have actually changed hands.

Tehran appears intent on formalizing that loophole: sources that spoke to Asharq al-Awsat relayed that Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf — one of Iran’s chief negotiators with the U.S. — visited Baghdad Wednesday and pitched a plan to conceal the factions’ heavier weapons or relocate them to Iran.

Three other, more powerful factions have not bothered with the theater at all. Kataib Hezbollah’s leader, Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi, has said flatly his group will not disarm, calling the recent U.S.-Saudi strikes on Iraq “a serious precedent that may establish a new phase in the region.” Washington, by the way, has a $10 million bounty on his head.

Harakat al-Nujaba and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada have taken similar hardlines, the former arguing that weapons are needed to “defend the holy sites of Iraq and its people.”

Indeed, since February 28, Iran-aligned factions have been blamed for repeated drone and missile strikes on Iraqi Kurdistan, which has long been a magnet for targets because of its close ties to the U.S. More consequentially, Saudi Arabia accused militias operating from Iraqi soil of launching drones at its oil infrastructure in late July, prompting joint Saudi-American strikes on Popular Mobilization Forces sites that killed roughly 20 fighters, including Iranian advisers.

Al-Zaidi cancelled a planned trip to Riyadh in protest. Then, in a smaller and more telling gesture, he received Riyadh’s intelligence chief in Baghdad instead and pledged that Iraqi territory would not be used to launch attacks on anyone.

Meanwhile, U.S. policy in Iraq, steered and articulated most clearly by Tom Barrack, does not view Iraq as a discrete problem so much as one node in an American project spanning Barrack’s three portfolios. He is ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Syria and Iraq, and he treats the Gulf states as an extension of the same brief, using them as a financing arm for reconstruction projects and loans for Damascus and Baghdad.

Iraq, as Barrack said after al-Zaidi’s visit to Washington, is “uniquely positioned to connect the region through deeper integration with the GCC, Türkiye, Syria, Jordan, Central Asia, the Balkans, and the Caucuses.” Iran is pointedly excluded from that list.

Barrack has spoken of wanting to make the Strait of Hormuz “an afterthought” within two years. He is betting on overland pipelines, such as the revived pipeline from Northern Iraq’s Kirkuk to Syria’s Baniyas port, and new capacity feeding Turkey’s Ceyhan terminal, which binds Iraqi crude to Ankara and Damascus and distances it from the Gulf.

While this vision is coherent, it requires Iraq’s own house to be in order first. But neither Tehran nor Baghdad’s most powerful political coalition seem prepared to allow that just yet.

The reality is that Iraq’s September 30 deadline is not really Iraq’s to keep. Whether Iran-backed militias disarm, freeze, or fight depends less on al-Zaidi’s pledges and legislative proposals than on decisions being made in Washington and Tehran regarding the ongoing war.

A war that drags on keeps Baghdad in financial distress and the militias’ argument for “resistance” alive. A deal that returns the U.S. and Iran to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding they signed in June, which suspended hostilities between them, could give al-Zaidi some room, but easing the pressure is not the same as solving the underlying problem.

Complete disarmament of the hardline factions requires two things not currently on offer: Iran deciding the militias are no longer worth protecting, and the Iraqi state actually using force against members of its own governing coalition. The former is unlikely, and the latter could be disastrous, risking precisely the civil war scenario analysts and even armed faction leaders have warned about.

item.title: Houthis may meet their match as Yemen slips back into civil war
item.description:
Yemen’s front lines have barely moved since the 2022 truce, but the war around them is changing.

Ballistic missiles and drones are striking far beyond established positions, and forces associated with the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government are responding more aggressively to infiltrations and military buildups. As commanders review readiness across key fronts, Yemen’s political leadership is signaling that attacks will no longer be absorbed without a response.

Together, the developments suggest that the country’s long period of “no war, no peace” may be coming to an end. There has been no ground offensive large enough to redraw the map so far. But war can return gradually as long-range strikes increase, forces reinforce positions and the rules of retaliation begin to change.

Mokha: War without taking territory


The Port of Mokha stopped operating two weeks ago amid repeated Houthi ballistic missile and drone attacks.

Dr. Abdulmalik al-Sharabi, director of the port, said the facility had been hit by more than 35 missile and drone strikes, concentrated on its economic zone, quay, logistics facilities, dredger, central workshop, administrative buildings and employee housing.

According to al-Sharabi, 16 people have been killed and 22 wounded, and the port is now closed to maritime traffic. Military information from the western coast puts the number of ballistic missiles and drones launched toward Mokha during the latest escalation at close to 90.

The attacks show how the conflict can inflict strategic damage without changing control of territory.

The Houthis do not need to seize the port by land to disrupt it. Striking the quay, logistics facilities and equipment can interrupt shipping and trade while imposing economic costs from a distance. A missile explodes in seconds; its economic impact can last far longer.

The influence of regional powers has contributed to this shifting picture within Yemen. Saudi Arabia remains the key supporter of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, providing political, financial, development and military backing. Saudi assistance has included support to the Central Bank and government finances to help cover public-sector salaries, while the Saudi Development and Reconstruction Program for Yemen has funded infrastructure, public services and reconstruction projects. Riyadh also continues to provide military support to forces aligned with the government, including the National Resistance Forces in Mokha and the Nation’s Shield Forces in Hadramout and Marib.

The wider confrontation involving Iran has added another layer to the conflict. The Houthis’ close alignment with Tehran means that pressure on Iran and changes in the regional balance of power can reverberate inside Yemen. The recent increase in Houthi missile and drone attacks may therefore reflect both the wider regional escalation and concern that stronger government-aligned forces could launch a broader offensive, prompting the Houthis to intensify attacks in an effort to deter or pre-empt such a move.

When the missile misses


These deep strikes are extending the geography of danger far beyond the front line. A Houthi ballistic missile recently crashed into a civilian home in al-Akamah village in Maqbanah district, west of Taiz. The home of Abdullah Ahmed al-Jabari was heavily damaged and livestock were killed, although initial information indicated no human casualties.

The missile was believed to have come from the direction of Ibb province or Sharab district and may have been heading toward Mokha, according to local residents who spoke on condition of anonymity. The house was in a Houthi-controlled area, underscoring how long-range weapons can endanger civilians even on the launch side when a missile malfunctions or falls short.

Taiz: The government's test


If Mokha shows the reach of Houthi firepower, Taiz tests whether government forces have become better prepared to contain pressure on the ground.

The commander of Yemen’s Fourth Military Region, Maj. Gen. Hamdi Hassan Shukri, recently met Taiz Axis commander Maj. Gen. Khaled Fadhel and unit commanders to review troop deployment, battlefield developments, frontline needs, coordination and permanent readiness.

After years of largely fixed front lines, the emphasis is increasingly on unifying efforts, integrating units and responding quickly to battlefield changes, according to Abdulrahman al-Yousifi, official spokesperson for the Taiz Military Axis.

Government forces have also been striking Houthi concentrations and buildups on the northern front while confronting infiltration attempts along contact lines.

Al-Yousifi said troops have repeatedly prevented Houthi fighters from penetrating their positions and have captured some infiltrators.

The military significance of his account lies in the nature of the fight. For now, Taiz is less about gaining territory than preventing the enemy from changing the map.

Government forces have improved their ability to detect Houthi reinforcements before they reach an assault position and strike concentrations of enemy troops early, before a local attack becomes a breakthrough. Years of stalemate have also given troops familiarity with roads, mountain approaches and likely infiltration routes.

That does not amount to strategic superiority. But it can make government defensive lines harder to break.

"The era of aggression without costs is over"


The most important change may be political rather than purely military.

Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, has said the government did not initiate the escalation but would no longer accept a situation in which the Houthis choose when and where to attack while expecting restraint once government forces respond. “The era of aggression without cost is over,” al-Alimi said.

If translated into military policy, that statement could mark a significant change in the rules of engagement. For years, limited attacks were often met with limited responses, allowing both sides to maintain an unstable but contained confrontation.

A policy of imposing a cost seeks to deter the other side by convincing it that every attack will carry consequences. But attempts to establish deterrence can backfire.

If the government believes stronger retaliation will force the Houthis to step back, while the Houthis believe greater missile pressure will force the government into restraint, both sides could escalate based on incorrect assumptions.

The danger may not be that either side has already decided on nationwide war, but that each believes it can escalate without triggering one.

The next war may look different


A renewed Yemeni war may not resemble the early years of the conflict. Ground offensives will still matter, particularly in strategic areas such as Marib, but fighting may increasingly be shaped by drones, ballistic missiles, artillery and attacks on logistics and economic infrastructure.

The critical questions may no longer be only who gains territory, but who can keep ports operating, protect supply routes, replace losses, bring in reinforcements and maintain coordination while several fronts come under pressure.

That is why readiness in Taiz, Marib, Hadramout and the western coast matters. The anti-Houthi camp’s central challenge is whether different forces can respond as parts of one military system if several fronts intensify simultaneously.

For now, Mokha is the warning and Taiz is the test. Mokha demonstrates how Houthi missiles and drones can impose military, economic and civilian costs without capturing territory. Preparations at Taiz will show whether government forces can turn years of static warfare into stronger defenses and prevent local attacks from becoming strategic breakthroughs.

Yemen’s front lines have not moved dramatically yet. But the rules that kept them frozen are beginning to change.

item.title: Syria says no Turkish military build-up planned at airbase struck by Israel
item.description:
Aug 20 (Reuters) - Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said he made clear to Israel there were no plans to establish a Turkish military base at Abu al-Duhur airbase, which Israel struck on Tuesday, saying the site was being rehabilitated for use by the Syrian Air Force.

Al-Shaibani said Turkish military officers had visited the base as part of training and broader military cooperation. He denied any Turkish military build-up, sayingthe facility was largely empty and not yet operational.

item.description:

SYDNEY, Aug 20 (Reuters) - Australia summoned Israel's ambassador on Thursday and expressed outrage at a decision by its military not to pursue criminal proceedings over the death of an Australian aid worker in a 2024 airstrike in Gaza.

The Israeli military said on Wednesday it had found no basis to investigate the killings of seven aid workers with the World Central Kitchen charity, including Australian Zomi Frankcom, after a fact-finding and assessment procedure.

item.title: 'More confrontational': Iran's new hardline security leadership

Khamenei, in power since his father Ali Khamenei was killed at the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran in February, has yet to be seen in public since taking on the top job and his health and influence remain uncertain.

item.title: Russia and Ukraine are sending assault groups deep behind enemy lines, blurring the front line
item.description: The nature of the war has changed once again. Not only in the rear, where the intensity of mutual strikes has increased and warehouses belonging to online marketplaces and other businesses have often become targets. There have also been changes at the front, in tactics. Traditional infiltration by small groups has reached a new level. Now assault units try to slip through undetected not for hundreds of meters, but for kilometers. Sometimes the depth of these raids exceeds 10 kilometers. The idea is that such groups do not require large amounts of supplies and can therefore operate cut off from the main forces. The raids destabilize the enemy’s defenses and can also be dangerous for its drone operators. This has created a new picture at the front: in many sectors, the battle formations of the two armies have become intermixed; control over roads and towns is often unstable; villages change hands several times a week.
